utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us how you saw Mr. Krnojelac when 75 detainees were taken away. Did you also see soldiers in the compound when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what became of these 75 detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what became of them. Out of those detainees, I don't know that anyone has been heard of since they were taken to the gate, and I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, as well, that you saw Mr. Krnojelac during a kind of alarm situation, alert situation. Do you recall when that was, when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when that happened. There was an alert, but I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time of the year it was? Was it more to the end of your confinement or in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in July or August, maybe even September. It was most probably in September, October. I don't know, but it wasn't in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it during daytime or more to the evening when that happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon. It was not evening yet. It was afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yesterday you also told us how you were interrogated and how Paprica told you that there was a Crisis Staff and they would decide, and the warden was in this Crisis Staff as well. When did Mr. Paprica tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that at my interrogation, when I was at his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the other persons, that is Starovic and Gagovic that you mentioned, were they also present when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Starovic, Paprica, Gagovic, and from time to time, Mitar Rasevic would come in. He was coming and going. I don't know whether Rasevic was there at the moment when he said it, but Starovic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the other -- that's Starovic and Gagovic, did they add to what Paprica told you or were they quiet?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember them saying anything. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yesterday you also told us when the journalists came to visit and filmed in the KP Dom, and you told us that the warden was present. Was he accompanying these journalists or what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present outside the gate within the compound. He was watching, but he was in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he come together with the journalists; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, right when the journalists came, the warden passed through the gate with them, and first they went together to the carpentry shop. When they came back from there, he was probably showing them around the premises and the compound, the yard of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he was probably showing them around. Did you see him going around?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in their company. I don't know what he was showing them. I don't know what he was doing, but he was in their company. He was together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac in the compound or in the building with military personnel?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building where the prisoners were, I never saw him there. In the yard I would see him with military men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who that was, these military men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him several times. Once I saw him passing through the courtyard together with Boro Ivanovic. On another occasion I saw him walking in the company of a military man. I don't know his rank, but before the war he was an economist. His name is Milos Dragicevic. And another man who wore a military uniform, wearing a yellow bag across the shoulder like officers, he used to be a male nurse at Maglic. He was Sipcic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Krnojelac with these military people, what were they doing? Were they just walking past the prisoners building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the gate, they passed by building 1 and building 2. Then they passed by the kitchen. They stood for a while outside the kitchen, talking. They walked about the courtyard. I don't know what they were discussing or what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Boro Ivanovic. Did you see him in the prison on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him often. He would be alone in the courtyard for the most part, and he talked to captive Serbian soldiers in the courtyard. Some of them were in uniform, some of them were in camouflage uniforms. He had arguments with them, loud arguments. We could hear that, but we couldn't hear what exactly they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ivanovic ever speak with the Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't have because all of them were in their rooms except for those who were cleaning the courtyard, and I never saw him talking to anyone of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Ivanovic ever enter the building where the Serb prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. At least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also saw Mr. Krnojelac in the company of a military person, Dragicevic. Do you know what position he had, Milos Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was. He wore a military uniform, but what his task was and what his position was, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This other person, Sipcic, do you know what his position was? In the military, I mean.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned that Mr. Gagovic was the deputy warden, and you said that he introduced himself as such. When you saw him, what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing trousers. I couldn't say what kind. He also had a short leather, yellow jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Savo Todovic. What was his exact function in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Todovic. I don't remember that man. They told me that there was a Savo Todovic and in all probability - I couldn't say for sure - he worked in the carpentry shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but we, the inmates, knew that he was the commander of the police, that is, the guards, commander of the guard, the entire guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him on a daily basis in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasevic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often. I don't know whether it was on a daily basis, but we saw him rather often.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he wear, what kind of clothing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform of the kind previously worn by policemen in the KP Dom. It was not a military uniform, it was a police one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic and the guards, did they attend to all detainees, that is, the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what they attended to, but the guards were also in charge of Serbian soldiers. They would let them out for lunch and take them back to their rooms, and during the day, these soldiers would walk around the courtyard. They would play football, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were detained in the KP Dom until 8 December 1992. How did you leave the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the KP Dom on the 8th of December. That morning, we went out to have breakfast. We lined up before entering the kitchen. It was a cold day. There were puddles from the rain the previous day and they were frozen. At that moment, a guard came with a list. He called out myself and some people who were also in my room. He told us to come out of the line, go back to our rooms and prepare for an exchange. I, together with two or three other men, went back to our rooms, whereas the others left for breakfast. We were told that we would have breakfast later, once we were prepared for the exchange. Later, when the other inmates came back to our room, we said our goodbyes, and we went down to the compound. We assembled in the canteen. We were given breakfast and after breakfast we lined up in front of the gate. We waited there, lined up, for about 10 or 15 minutes, and then we were taken out outside the gate; there we were inspected. The guards inspected what we had on us. They were looking for pieces of paper, notes. They took away these things and threw them away. I had some recipes for growing tomatoes or flowers. Those were some things I just did to spend time. And we had some pieces of bread that were given to us by the cooks before we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we would not need all the details. We have already noticed that you have a memory for -- you have a very detailed memory, but we would not need all these details. Who took you over when you went through the KP Dom, when you went outside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A van pulled up backwards, a Deutz, that was the type of vehicle, some sort of pick-up, with the roof opened, with chairs on the both sides of it, and some soldiers who wore olive-green/grey uniforms and camouflage uniforms listed us first. Then they searched us again. The bread that I had was taken away by them and thrown away, and then they put us on the van. They seated us six on each side, and we sat there inside the vehicle while they were handling some papers, some paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that they listed you first. Does that mean that they put your names down on a list or what? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they did. They made a list of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said they were handling some paperwork. What kind of paperwork was it? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. They had some papers in their hands. They listed us one by one and we got on board the vehicle. I don't know what kind of papers those were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they hand over some papers to the KP Dom staff or did they get papers from them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I cannot say one way or another. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had boarded the vehicle, a soldier got on in the back and another got on in front. We were 12 of us and two of them, totalling 14. They pulled down this roof, and we set off. We didn't know where we were going. They would stop occasionally. We didn't know where we were. So it continued until a place where we stopped. They took off -- they took down the roof and we looked around. I assumed that we were in the village of Mrezica, also known as Ovsiji. I should also like to mention that from the moment we left the KP Dom, we were continuously beaten. One of the soldiers beat us all the time and, from time to time, the other one who had a hat on his head and was nicknamed Vojvoda, would beat us too. Then When we stopped at that place and when they took down the roof, I saw them talking beside the car. I saw torched houses around. Then they threw in a leg of a calf which was not properly skinned and they made us eat it. They forbade us to eat the dirty piece of hoof on that leg. I was blood-soaked. My nose was broken, and we were all beaten on our backs. At that moment, the man who drove the van came in to see what's going on. He had a long beard, and he ordered the soldiers to throw the leg out. He told them to leave us alone, and then we continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. I just want to check something with you because in the transcript, it says they forbade us to eat the dirty piece of hoof.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Where were you taken? Where did this drive end?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where they took us after that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to Kalinovik. That's where they took us from there. In Kalinovik, we stopped outside a building of some kind. They took the roof down, and the bearded man carrying the machine-gun brought us some bread. We were still hungry, so he brought more bread. Some soldiers and some women came and looked at us. The women told the soldiers not to beat us. We looked very miserable. And we continued on our way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. We do not need all these details. Where were you kept in Kalinovik, in which building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kalinovik, I don't know exactly the name of that place, but it was a powder factory. There was a ramp there which they opened. They let us enter the building. They told us we would be accommodated there. It was a huge place, this powder factory, and there were wooden pallets there in one corner. We got about a dozen of dirty blankets, some mattresses which were also dirty, and they told us we would sleep there. They told us also that we would get dinner and that's where we would stay. When we tried to make some beds for the 12 of us, we discovered the place was mice infested and the mice were running around everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you again. We would not need these details. How long did you stay in Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Kalinovik on the 12th of December, and I -- I'm sorry. I arrived on the 8th of December and was exchanged on the 12th, which means within three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know for whom you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were exchanged one by one. The first man was exchanged on the 10th, the second one on the 11th, and I was exchanged on the 12th. I don't know for whom I was exchanged. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We have already talked about your physical suffering during your detention. Did you suffer psychological consequences due to the living conditions and what you have survived in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still suffer those consequences. After my release from the KP Dom, I underwent thorough medical examinations in Split. When I arrived in Split, I weighed 54 kilos. The time when we left Kalinovik was the hardest time of all in my life. I was running a high fever. I had diarrhea, vomiting. When I arrived at the hospital, they told me I would probably die. They couldn't give me a drip. They gave me some medication and tried to transfer me to Split in a hurry, but I arrived in Split only on the 12th of December, where I was hospitalised. I got treatment there and underwent examinations which revealed a vitaminosis. My entire body was black and blue. I had discoloration on my entire body. My hands and feet were swollen. They told me I had a dislodged kidney and some cysts. They made scans of my brain, and they said that with good exercise and good treatment, I could get better. I had to climb the mount Marijan almost every day and to eat as much fruit as I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. How long were you hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. For about ten days. As long as the examinations took. And among the consequences I still suffer from the camp are nightmares. Whenever I sleep, I dream about the traumas I have experienced. I cry out, yell, holler during the night and it's very embarrassing. When I move about in the street, if I'm walking alone and somebody is walking behind me, I have a feeling that that person behind me would attack me, would drive a knife in my back, and I always step aside and let that person pass me by to avoid having to go through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These are the questions that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I'm one of the Defence counsel for the accused, Mr. Krnojelac. First of all, I would like to ask you to make a pause after each question I ask so that the interpreters can interpret the question. Until now, the questions were asked in English and you received the interpretation immediately and you could answer immediately, but now I would like you to make a pause after my question and answer only after a pause. Sir, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 21st and 22nd October, 1995, on the subjects you have testified about today?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this statement in 1990 -- I don't remember the year, but I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also true that on the 12th of December, 1992, you gave a statement to the public security station in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't on the 12th. It was on the 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were these statements read to you and did you sign them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were read to me and I signed them. Actually, I don't know whether I signed them or not, but they were read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So those are statements that you made voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As your own statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, during the examination-in-chief, you talked about the very beginning of the conflict in Foca. I'm going to ask you something that you already spoke about in your statements. I'll ask you whether this is correct and whether you still maintain that. You said that in Foca, the first political meeting was a rally of the Party of Democratic Action on the banks of the Drina River and that 100.000 people assembled on that occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the first meeting on the banks of the Drina River, and I don't know exactly whether there were 100 [sic] people. Rumour had it that there were 100 [sic] people. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said exactly that this was a very big rally and that it was attended by 100.000 people.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably so. I didn't do any counting, but rumour had it that there were 100 [sic] people, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You'll have to pause just a little bit longer than you're pausing, sir. The interpreters work about half a sentence behind you. So just wait a little bit longer before you start your answer to the questions. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you something about the transcript. I put my question asking 100.000 people, but the transcript says 100.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the witness said invariably "100" only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreters just said that's precisely what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Both times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both times say the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Then my question is are we talking about 100.000 people or are we talking about 100 people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you stated that this rally was attended by Muslims from all over Bosnia, Sandzak, that Croats came from Zagreb and Bosnia, and Muslims from Croatia and that they attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from. Muslims came most probably from all over Bosnia. I don't know about that. I cannot say where they came from because I was not on any committee or something. I did not read anything. I don't know it all, where they came from and who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am reading to you what you wrote in your statement.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that they came from Croatia, from all over Bosnia, there were stories to that effect. Most probably they did, but I don't know exactly. It's not really that important, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you stated that at that meeting that Bosnian and Croat flags were tied together?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I stated that. I don't remember that, but there were some that were tied together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why was the Serb flag not tied together with these two?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read to you exactly what you said in your statement and then you're going to tell me whether that is correct or not by way of commenting on what we have just been saying. "The Serbs were very irritated and dissatisfied with this rally. The relations between the Serbs and the Muslims worsened."

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer now? That is correct. I had socialised with the Serbs, my colleagues. They told me that they were really irritated by this and they were unhappy about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After that, did a Serb rally follow at the football stadium that was much smaller than this one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer now? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, since you are asking me all the time whether you can answer now, if you want to, you can look at me and I'll give you a sign with my hand and then you can answer. Perhaps that's going to be easier and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. faster. Thank you. Before the war conflict broke out was there dissatisfaction among Serbs in town because the Muslims starting withdrawing their children from the Yugoslav People's Army? Did you talk about that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Serbs organised a public rally on the main square in the centre of Foca. The main topic at the rally was why were the Muslims not joining the army. Before that you said that Muslim mothers and parents took their children out of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was, but I did not attend the rally. That's what people talked about, but I was not at the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, what you said is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before the war conflict broke out, do you know that the Muslim side had a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On page 5 of your statement you said, "Radio Sarajevo reported that the Muslim Crisis Staff and the Muslim defenders had fled to Ustikolina." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The radio said that they had withdrawn to Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement during the examination-in-chief, sir, you said that on Tuesday, the 7th of April, you went from Jelec to Foca, to work.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Set out to Foca to work? Yes, that's correct. I don't know whether it was the 6th or the 7th too or whatever, but that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Then you returned to Jelec so that you would not remain in Foca if there were to be roadblocks that would prevent you from getting out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that I went to Foca on the Tuesday. That was the 7th most probably. After that, when there was nothing to do at my working place, I returned home around 11.00 or 12.00. My wife --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, we heard about that. I'm just asking you whether it is correct that on the same day you left Foca and went back to Jelec once again so that road blocks would not keep you in Foca. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did your children remain in Jelec or did they go out to Foca with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed in Jelec. They were not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Didn't you go to school? Didn't your children go to school?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The children did not go to school on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why did you go to school to teach and you did not let your own children go to school?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take them for safety reasons. They stayed back. They did not come with me; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that you were told in Jelec that you would get a rifle. Did you get a rifle in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get a rifle. Nobody told me that they'd give me a rifle, and I didn't get one anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that the locals in Jelec agreed on a hand-over of weapons and that everything could be dealt with peaceably. Is it correct that Besevic convinced the people of Jelec not to hand over weapons but to join in the arms struggle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend this meeting. As far as I heard, when Besevic came, he said that whoever wants to can join him and who doesn't want to doesn't have to. It was up to everyone individually. He did not come to defend Jelec. He came to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that day, when weapons had to be handed over by 12.00, Besevic arrived in the morning and that is how this plan concerning the hand-over of weapons went down the drain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many soldiers did Besevic have with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a camouflage uniform and four or five soldiers. With him were five or six or ten - I don't know exactly - people in civilian uniforms, and they also carried hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you said you had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you arrested with that pistol on you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested with that pistol on me, and I can also tell you all about how I was arrested. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please, just tell me whether you had a pistol on you when you were arrested or not.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested, I did not have a pistol on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you now the statement you gave to the public security station in Trnovo or, actually, just part of that statement. "Jasmin Beckovic frisked me, and he found my own pistol on me. It was a CZ pistol, 62 millimetre. He took it away from me and he put it on his own belt, and he also took a knife away from me."

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Jasmin frisked me, he only found a knife on me. There was no pistol. When they were pushing me ahead of themselves as a human shield in front of their lines, I came to a place where we had lain as we were hiding from grenades and weapons. They were digging up the place where we were and they were torching it. Then there was the blouse of a man who was lying there with us and in his pocket he found a pistol magazine, and Jasko said, "You have a pistol. You have to give me a pistol or I'll kill you straight away." I said to him that when I was running with my children, 100 metres above that I took my pistol off and put it under a rock. That's where the pistol remained. And I said that it was there. Why did I leave it? My daughter was not there. I didn't want to carry a pistol with me. I went back to look for my daughter, so I went without a pistol, without any weapons, and he arrested me without a pistol, without any weapons, and from there he took me to that place where the rock was and then we took the pistol from underneath the rock and I handed it over to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, are you a huntsman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fond of fishing. I have been a sports fisherman since 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, during the examination-in-chief, that you had binoculars. How come you had binoculars?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had binoculars that my daughter got as a present from a relative of ours from Germany. It was a small pair of binoculars for soccer games. This was a little present that she had got. She is the one who carried it around. She had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You did not have it on you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she had it. When they captured her, they found that pair of binoculars and they took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that you used binoculars to watch.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when shells were falling on Jelec. We were getting out of this thicket, because we were there on the 1st and 2nd and 3rd of May. We went out to a meadow. Both the children and I used the very same binoculars to watch shells falling on Jelec.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you did not have binoculars on you, why did this person who arrested you say, "Here comes the scout?" Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had probably assumed that there were some military men up there and that's why they said that I was a scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, why did you say to the public security station that you had the pistol on you, that it was found on you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was on me. I carried it with me, but under these circumstances, it was not directly on me, as I have already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The person you mentioned as Jasmin Beckovic, what's he from an ethnic point of view?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he take you prisoner?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When these men appeared, this firing squad, they called it the comb. There were 20 to 30 soldiers uphill and downhill. They put all their rifles up on the ready, and the one who was holding me at gunpoint ordered Jasmin Beckovic to frisk me. He walked up to me, frisked me. He took off my trousers, my boots. He only found my knife, took away my knife, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We heard about that. I just wanted to know what Jasmin Beckovic was by ethnicity, and he was among the persons who arrested you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not recognise him at that moment, and when the other man grabbed me by the neck and tried to kill me, and then he said, "Do you know me?" and I said that I did know him. He introduced himself, saying that his name was Jasmin Beckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And he's an ethnic Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday, sir, that together with you were women, children, and elderly men, that they were with you and that they were arrested with you. Where were the younger men from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As people were fleeing the village, I don't know where they scattered about in these forests. Husad Cesalj, Siljevac there were mountains and forests all around. I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, you are starting your answers to the questions too early. Just wait that little bit longer. Mr. Bakrac has offered to give you a hand signal, which seems like a good idea, because he knows when the translation is finished because he is listening to it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about these young men from Jelec? Did they go -- did they follow Besevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in town, Besevic went uphill from Jelec. He said that whoever wanted to join him could. Whoever wanted to join him could and who didn't want to didn't have to. I saw two or three young men who did come with me. That's what I did see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's what you saw, right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you mentioned Cosovic. What was he, a civilian or which rank did he hold if he was a military person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at Brod. When we were brought there -- I mean I had known Cosovic from before. He had a camouflage uniform. I don't know his first name. He had a military camouflage uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was this a uniform belonging to the ordinary army or the military police or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the ordinary army or whatever. I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you recognised Cosovic. He was commander of the military police and he was a former pupil of mine from school. What is correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that Cosovic was a former pupil of mine. He Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. went to school to become a waiter and that's what he did. When I was detained, when I came to the camp, we heard this in the camp, that Cosa was commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zelja Jankovic and a third person who were present there. What were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovic -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you recognised Zelja Jankovic and that you knew the third person by sight. What were the three of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had camouflage uniforms. I don't know what they were, but they all had camouflage uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave in 1995, you said, "The three of them were members of the military police."

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably they were members. Since Cosa was, they were too, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, what was the maximum of persons detained in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I speak now? In my room, Room 18, in the month of June or it was the end of June, the largest number of persons detained there was 70 to 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what was the biggest number of persons who were ethnic Muslims who were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually did the counting. In my room, we tried to keep abreast of this. We think that the peak was reached when the number was 780. However, our figures did not match. It wasn't one person who was doing the counting, it was groups of people, two by two by four. So our figures did not match. There was a margin of 20. So it was between 780 and 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said, "In my room, the largest number of detainees ever was up to 80 and the largest number of prisoners in the prison was, to the best of my knowledge, 600 at the end of June."

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the statement's wrong. I remember well that two men were doing the counting, that they counted the people who were going out of building 1 when they were going in groups to have lunch. Then we added up all the members of these groups. Then other people were counting men as they were getting out of our building, going out for breakfast and lunch. So we counted all the people in these groups and we added all of this up, and the grand total was about 750, 780. So our figures did not correspond. Invariably there was a margin of 20 or 30. So then we also came to the figure concerning the number of persons who were in solitary confinement and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You don't have to explain all of this to me. Please just be so kind as to tell me the following: What you said in 1995 and what you are saying now, in 2001, which one is correct? Is it 600 or is it 780? And did you come to this figure because you subsequently talked to some persons about the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any subsequent conversations. That's not how I got this number. I'm saying that I should have said in my first statement that it was 780. How come they got this figure 600, I don't know. Maybe they made a mistake as they were writing this down. That might be an error as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yesterday during your examination-in-chief, and you repeated the same thing again today, you said that you saw Warden Krnojelac with journalists within the compound and that he was wearing a military uniform and carrying a pistol. Did you mention earlier in your statement given to the OTP the visit of these journalists?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I did. Maybe I forgot. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the visit of journalists in your statement made to the OTP, did you ever mention this fact that Warden Krnojelac was with them? Did you ever mention it before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I did, but I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you now a brief sentence. "Two days before they came, the detainees were told to clean their rooms. They gave us haircuts and shaves, and we were taken for a bath. I saw British journalists from the window of my room. They were talking to detainees on the ground floor, offering them cigarettes, until the Serbs came and stopped the filming because the detainees were sticking their hands out of the window in order to get some cigarettes because everybody wanted them." When you mention this visit of the British journalists, why did you not mention what you said today for the first time in 2001, that you saw Warden Krnojelac with them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't remember it then. Perhaps it didn't occur to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Will you tell me, please, did you speak to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor about your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but most probably I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Regarding this interrogation, did you ever before mention to the Office of the Prosecutor that one of the investigators told you that Milorad Krnojelac was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I'm 100 per cent sure, but I most probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have the Official Gazette of the municipality of Foca and the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff. I'm asking you, are you sure the investigator told you who the member of the Crisis Staff were and that Milorad Krnojelac was among them.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintain that is so, 1 million per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will read out to you now what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor. On page 3, there is one sentence only and I will read slowly. "I heard later from other prisoners in the KP Dom that members of the Crisis Staff in Foca were the following: Vojo Maksimovic, Velibor Ostojic, Dr. Mandic, Miro Stanic, and Cedo Zelovic." You never mentioned Milorad Krnojelac anywhere, and that was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I give that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You gave that statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I forgot. Maybe I forgot to mention it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you remembered it now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you want to answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question was: And you remembered it now? We still have no answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me, please, what it is that jogged your memory and made you remember that fact?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What made me remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, now in 2001.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What reminded me is when I was giving the statement at Paprica's, in his office. Paprica told me that, "This statement that you gave is no good at all. You haven't said a thing. If you come for an interrogation again, you'll get a good beating. This will be reviewed by the Crisis Staff. We are drafting it in five or six copies." And he mentioned where the copies were going. I don't remember that part now. Then Vojo said at that moment, "I know this man. He's telling the truth. He wasn't involved in anything. He wasn't mixed up in anything," and he said, "If the Crisis Staff returns this statement, you'll get a good beating." And these people, and I don't remember all of them, that was the end of it. Then Paprica said, "You'll give me the details now." They gave me the statement for me to read. I had no glasses on me so I couldn't see enough to read and I told them so. Vojo took the statement from me and said, "Everything is written here exactly as you said it and everything that you said has been recorded." The sheet was filled out on one side and almost filled out on the other side, and he showed me a space where I was supposed to sign it. He said, "But please sign your full name and surname to fill the space completely so that nobody can add anything later," and that was the end of my interrogation, and I signed that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How come you didn't remember all these details in 1995? Because you spoke about this interrogation and mentioned that you were interrogated in the administrative building by Starovic and Paprica, and you didn't remember a single detail about how you were interrogated. When you were enumerating the members of the Crisis Staff, you didn't mention the fact that Milorad Krnojelac was one of them, nor did you mention in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor your interrogation, when speaking about your interrogation at Paprica's, you didn't mention even then that you had learned that Milorad Krnojelac had been a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the only thing I failed to mention was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You didn't mention anything. You didn't mention that Starovic or Paprica had told you about that.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Starovic told me to sign my full name and surname. You mean I didn't mention that in my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what they recorded there. I don't know whether all that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the help of the usher, I would like to show this witness the Official Gazette of the municipality of Foca and the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff. I would like the witness to have a look at this and see if Milorad Krnojelac is on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I really don't think that this witness is the appropriate person to be proving this document. It's never been suggested that he saw it. May I suggest that the more appropriate course is either to show him his statement to get him to agree that none of those things are in it or ask the Prosecution whether it accepts that the statement does not contain that material. The simplest procedure, if I may suggest, is the second one. It saves an enormous amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. I decided on the spur of the moment to show him these papers, but I agree. He may not be the best person to show them to. This piece of evidence will wait for its turn. I agree that the Office of the Prosecutor, as you had suggested -- I'm sorry. It seems to me I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I was going to say you can tender that document, the Official Gazette, at any time that you want to. The Prosecution will either require you to prove it properly if they have some problem with it or they will accept it, and you can put documents into evidence now. But I don't think that there's any point in asking this witness about it because you haven't suggested to him that he ever saw that. He is simply relying upon what somebody told him. What that person told him may not have been correct. You proceed how you wish, but that is the way I suggest that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, did you mention at any time before yesterday's examination-in-chief that you knew that Milorad Krnojelac was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from everyone -- I don't know about everyone, actually, but rumour had it at the camp that the people mentioned were on the Crisis Staff together with the warden of the camp, Milorad Krnojelac. It's not only something that I invented, as you seem to be insinuating, many people at the camp knew that he was on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why didn't you ever say this before? That's my question. Do you agree that you failed to mention this in all of your previous statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Speaking to the Office of the Prosecutor of the security services centre, did you mention at any time before that you had seen Milorad Krnojelac at that drill that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I did; maybe I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said during your examination-in-chief yesterday that you saw Krnojelac wearing a uniform worn by officers. How do you distinguish between uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said yesterday exactly was that he was wearing a soldier's uniform, olive-green/grey, and that it was more like the one worn by noncommissioned officers in the Yugoslav People's Army. It's more like an officer's uniform, not a soldier's uniform. I said a NCO or an officer's uniform but not the soldier's uniform, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I asked. What are the characteristics on the basis of which you distinguish between uniforms? How did you decide that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This uniform, olive-green/grey, the cloth is of better quality, whereas the soldier's uniform is made of regular material used for soldiers. We all know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, do you mean to say that from your window you could see that the difference in cloth?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that, of course, even from a window. You can see that from a plane. Of course I saw it. This is a provocative question. I can see the difference in cloth. You know what a soldier's uniform is and what an officer's uniform is. You know exactly what NCOs wear, what officers wear, and what soldiers wear. This one definitely was the kind worn by NCOs or officers, but no way it was the soldier's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did it have any insignia?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I didn't even say I did. He had a belt and he had a pistol in his belt on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The uniforms of a regular soldier and the uniforms of NCOs or officers, are they different in terms of insignia?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are, but I couldn't see the insignia. I couldn't see any signs of rank. I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you saw the difference in cloth and you couldn't see the insignia. You didn't even notice whether there were any.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I didn't notice; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What did it consist of, this NCO or officer's uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trousers, shirt, belt, pistol, shoes. I don't know what kind of footwear. I don't know whether he wore a cap or not, whether he was bareheaded or not. I don't remember that. I just remember the trousers, the shirt, the belt, the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said yesterday and again today that you saw Krnojelac in the courtyard when there was this big exchange of 75 men. Did you remember that today? Is it one more thing that you remembered today? Because you never mentioned it before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, and I'm saying this again, I said it yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please, sir, don't. Please don't repeat what you said yesterday. We know what you said yesterday. I'm asking you why you had never mentioned it before, either to the Office of the Prosecutor or the secure services centre in Trnovo. Did you remember that just yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said it because nobody ever asked me, and it's not important. He could have been there and he didn't have to. We didn't go into all these details before. Nobody ever asked me, for instance, how many people had left on that occasion. They simply didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the Office of the Prosecutor didn't ask you for any details and did not inquire into matters regarding Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the statements you gave before.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the kind of detail we're going into here. I probably didn't remember all the things and they didn't ask about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mean they didn't ask you about Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they didn't. In fact, I don't remember. I can't possibly remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please tell me, since you mentioned he was passing by the metal door, is that the only exit out of the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main entrance to the compound is the only one, although there is another one near the carpentry shop, but it's mostly used by vehicles, trucks, cars, et cetera. But people used the main entrance, the metal door to the building whenever there were exchanges and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it another thing that you remembered only today that you saw the warden with Boro Ivanovic, Sipcic, and Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me about that, and if I didn't mention it before, that's why I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you remembered it only today.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I've always remembered it and I've always kept it in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether Ibrahim Sandal was beaten at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was he in the KP Dom when you were brought?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived in the KP Dom, as I said yesterday, ten days or 15 days or five days after me. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief yesterday, you said, sir, that you heard from a woman about the disappearance of 12 persons. When did you hear that from the woman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean you want the details?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I don't want the details. I'm only asking you: Can you tell me when you heard this from her?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this when I arrived in Split. People called me in Split, people who were looking for their relatives, husbands, friends. They were inquiring about the fate of the people who had been at the camp, and I said I knew those people and that they had stayed behind me at the camp. And since those people knew it, I will tell you clearly what that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, sir. My only question was: When did you hear from that woman about the 12 people? So it was after your release, after you were in Split.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Split. It was in January or February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about Dzemo Balic. Did you ever mention before that Dzemo Balic had told you about that young man in the solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before. I don't know exactly. I most probably did, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, you didn't mention it before.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man in the solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't remember it, so that's probably why I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said there existed two men named Balic. What were their first names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I know was Dzemo. He was in my room. And another Balic, when he was brought in and taken across the courtyard, he was badly beaten up, black and blue, and there were three or four other people with him brought from the village of Marinkovici. One of them was Hasanbegovic, another was Deluet. They didn't come to my room. They crossed the yard and were taken to solitary cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know that Balic from before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I knew Dzemo. I didn't know the other one. I just knew his name was Balic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You heard that from people in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You spoke about a person nicknamed Triva. Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Obren Obrenovic, a guard at the KP Dom camp. I know that he graduated from medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't need his personal details. Just please tell me: Where did he get his nickname Triva? Are you sure it was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We generally called him Triva. All of them had nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said he was the only one who had a wooden club.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the only one we saw in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: He was the only one among the guards? You didn't see anyone else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the windows in the prisoners' quarters were covered by paper sheets?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were some windows in the prisoners' quarters white-washed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been painted over before in white paint. That's how we found them. Nobody painted the windows while we were there. The paint was whitish grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there paint on the window panes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But there were paper sheets?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some places there were window panes, and where window panes were broken, paper sheets were glued. In the former times, there were some drawings on the wall, and when the windows were broken, we would take these drawings off the walls and use them to paste over the windows. That's what we did to close the windows to keep at least a little warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You spoke, sir, about Halim Dedovic. Was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there another Halim Dedovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I know this Halim Dedovic personally. He is a barber from Foca. I know him well. I don't know any other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said in your statement given to the OTP, "On another occasion, Nedzib Babalija, Murat Durgut, Ibrahim Sandal, and Halim Dedovic were taken out of my room and taken to the administrative building and beaten up."

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention Halim Dedovic as being taken from my building ever nor were any of them ever taken out. Halim Dedovic wasn't, Durgut wasn't, and Nedzib Babalija wasn't. Nedzib Babalija came to my room in Miljevina, and he was the one who came all beaten up. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you also mentioned in the same place that they were taken out to the administration building, and you said, "They told me about it when they came back." What is true? Did you make a mistake then or was your statement misrecorded by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying now is true. I don't remember what I said before. They were brought to my room from Miljevina. Mujo Durgut --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please don't repeat this. So what is here in the statement you gave to the OTP is not correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were taken to the gate for a beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, and that they were brought back to your room and that they told you about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that they were not taken out to the gate to be beaten and then brought back. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, that might be a good place to pause. I remind you that where a witness does not accept what you put to him about his statement, you're going to have to establish that fact. We do not want these statements in just to prove that fact. May I suggest that you ask the Prosecution informally to agree that what you have put is accurate about the statement and then that can be recorded and we're not then flooded with paper. If there is no agreement, then the document will have to go in for that purpose, but you can't merely just assert something to a witness and then tell us later that that is so unless there is some proof of it. We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in view of the suggestion you made before the break, I am going to formally ask the Prosecution whether they agree with the fact that they -- the witness did not mention in his statement that Milorad Krnojelac had been with the journalists who came to the KP Dom, also that he did not mention that the investigator told him that Milorad Krnojelac was a member of the Crisis Staff, that he did not mention this at all in his statements, also that he did not mention that he had seen Milorad Krnojelac in the afternoon when there was a state of emergency, that this was not mentioned in his statement, and also that he did not mention that he saw Milorad Krnojelac at all with Ivanovic Dragicevic and Sipcic, the military men, which is what he mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this will save an awful lot of time, but do give the Prosecution warning you are going to ask them so they can check themselves in the statements. You proceed with the cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry. I would just like to add one more thing. Before the break, we talked about an incident that the witness mentioned during the examination-in-chief, and I pointed out to him that in the statement that he made to the Office of the Prosecutor, he said that Nedzib Babalija, Murat Durgut Ibrahim Sandal, and Halim Dedic were taken out of his room and taken to the administration building and beaten up, and he said that they told him that when they were brought back. I would like to ask the Office of the Prosecutor to tell me whether they can agree that this is the statement that the witness did make in 1995. This is page 10 in the B/C/S version. I think that it is page 11 in the English version. Yes. Yes, 11 in the English version, paragraph number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall continue with the witness now. I think we'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You talked about an incident when a person called Salkic or Sacic transmitted messages. You said that this person passed messages to Muratovic and Malkic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also said that he was in building 1.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Salkic, Sacic. You also said that Muratovic and Malkic were in the room above you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your room? How come Salkic then passed massages to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I explain this in detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please don't do it in detail. Just tell us how he passed messages.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have to give a few sentences. From one floor, he would let a thread fall down to the ground floor and a little piece of paper was tied to that thread. A guard, Elcic, noticed that little piece of paper and he took it. He asked Sacic immediately what this was all about. When he brought him, he said that he was passing this message to another man, that he had some news as to what was going on. I don't know what kind of message it was. When they called him in for questioning, they asked him whether there was any anybody else who passed messages that way. He spoke up and said that in our building, it was done by Malkic and Avdo Muratovic. Then they called Avdo Muratovic and Malkic in for an interrogation to that room in my building, that guards' room down in the -- down on the ground floor, and Muradif Music was there also. So they were interrogated there and asked what this was all about, how they were doing this, and that was the problem. They beat them there and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, in the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you did speak about this incident, but you said that he was beaten up in relation to this incident, that is to say, a person whose name is on that sheet of paper that is in front of you. I can't remember the number of the exhibit. And that person is mentioned as your relative.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my relative?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't that time, and it was not mentioned that he was beaten up with regard to this particular subject. It wasn't my relative then. My relative was not there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your relative was involved. I'm going to read it to you. You also mentioned that they sent messages to one another. I'm going to read this to you now. It's on page number 10 of the B/C/S version, seventh paragraph: "One day, Avdo Muratovic, Sacic, Fahrudin Malkic, and" I am not going to read that name. That person is marked as your relative, "were beaten by a guard, Obren Obrenovic, when they were noticed passing messages to one another from the upper floor to the lower floor. I saw them being beaten in the room in our building which was used by the guards as an office." Is this correct what you stated to the OTP or is what you said today correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said to the OTP is correct, but my relative was not involved. My relative was not involved. I did not mention him before either as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's not the only difference. You also said they were beaten up because they were passing messages to one another. Today you told a different story.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I told a different story? I said that they sent messages to one another, Sacic, Malkic, Avdo, and Sacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, how could they send messages to one another when Sacic was in a completely different building? And now you said that he was sending a message to the ground floor and that he also spoke up and said that the others were doing that too. That's what you said a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Here you say that these people were exchanging messages between themselves, sending messages to one another?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they did that. Sacic was sending this message to the ground floor, down to the yard, and who he was passing this message to, I don't know. But then when he was being interrogated about this, he also said that Avdo and Malkic were doing such things as well. That's what I said, that's what's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I remind you, sir. You really must wait before you start your answer. You are making it very difficult for the interpreters. We want to know what you say, but we will not hear it if you interfere with the interpreters' job. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In line with your suggestion, I'm going to formally ask the Prosecutor whether they agree that in his statement given to the OTP, the witness did mention his relative as being involved in this incident and that he did notice that these people were sending messages to one another from the upper floor to the lower floor. That is page number 10 or, rather, page number 11 in the B/C/S version -- sorry, in the English version, page 11 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The cousin is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wonder, Mr. Bakrac, how important this particular dispute is, but I rely upon you to pick the ones which are important and not dwell upon these somewhat more incident the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you mentioned that Halim Konjo was taken out to be beaten up. Was he taken out on his own?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halim Konjo was not taken out on his own exactly on the night between the 12th and the 13th of June. I don't know exactly. And Uzinovic must have been the one who was also there and also the one who was commander of the traffic police, Nurko Nisic. From that day onwards, people were not taken out individually. Two, three, four were taken out, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you said to me or, rather, yesterday said during the examination-in-chief that Nurko Nisic was taken out the other day, not the same day as Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying he had to be taken out the same day with Halim Konjo. If not the same day, he could have been taken out, two, three, four, five days later, but at any rate, he was taken out during the first six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out to you what you have said, what you said to the OTP in your statement. "On the 12th of June, around 9.00 or 10.00 p.m., four detainees why taken out." So you mentioned the exact time and date. Four prisoners: Their names are Halim Konjo, Nurko Nisic, Zulfo Veiz, and Munib Veiz.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this is correct, that they were taken out on the 12th, these four persons, together?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever mention before in any one of your statements, either to the public security station or to the investigators of the OTP, that you heard that Milorad Krnojelac said that the KP Dom would be closed down, that some persons would be set free, others would be exchanged, and yet others would be transferred to other camps. Did you ever state that before to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before? I'm not sure, but I most probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please formally agree with me. Did the witness ever mention in the statements given to the OTP this particular distinction between such persons, that Milorad Krnojelac ever mentioned this to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's not mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: However, Your Honour, just one additional remark. The witness said he never heard Krnojelac say that, he said Paprica told him about these details, not Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the evidence you mean. There is reference to the incident at all in the statement. Thank you

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the usher please help me and place photograph 407477 on the ELMO. That is the lower photograph. The photograph bears the number 407477. It's the one below.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could the witness please show me the windows from where he heard, as he said, all these beatings that were taking place in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
