utterances.text: Do you want me to tell you where the window of my room is, where I was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Can you show the window of the room from where these beatings were heard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's either one or the other, this one or that one, but this first one most probably. This is the door where you enter, and these are the windows on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the transcript, I'm saying that the witness is pointing on photograph 407477 to the first and second windows to the left from the metal door that is the entrance into the administration building from the yard of the prison. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO the floor plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, please, before we move on to this question, tell me, these windows that you pointed to, those are the windows that you heard the sounds of beatings from and Halim Konjo, Nurko Nisic, Munib Veiz and Zulfo Veiz were taken out of there, right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did I hear this? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. But I'm asking whether these sounds came from those rooms that you just pointed out on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the rooms I just pointed out on the photograph, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you are coming in too early. Please pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. I shall bear this in mind. Sir, this is a floor plan. On the ELMO there is a floor plan of the KP Dom. I'm interested in the following: Can you show me the office or, rather, the place where you were interrogated or interviewed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really find my way on this photograph. I don't know how to do that. But I can describe to you where I was because I am familiar with the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you passed through the metal door into the hallway -- when you went to the main gate, did you go to the left part of the administrative building or the right part?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left one, upstairs. The left one. When I went out, I passed first the metal door and then yet another door and then we came to the exit from this building. When we reached the exit, then I was supposed to go left. I was supposed to go left when I was taken for an interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's in the same part that you pointed to when you said that that's where you heard the beatings from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When entering from the external part of the building, when actually you enter the KP Dom from the outside, these windows where they were beaten are on the right-hand side. However, when I was taken for interrogations, I was taken to the left side and I was taken upstairs. Upstairs, one floor up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Despite your promise to keep it in mind, Mr. Bakrac, on both times, both questions, you came in too early. It really does make it difficult, so please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, sir, you were interrogated in the part of the building that is opposite that part of the administrative building where you pointed out that the beatings took place.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you go out of the prison, out of the yard, on the left-hand side, when you enter from the outside, when you enter the prison from the outside, the rooms for beatings were on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That is to say that the place where you were interrogated and interviewed is in the opposite part of the administration building as compared to the premises where the beatings took place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we get out of the prison, we pass through halls, and at the very exit out of the KP Dom there are stairs that take you upstairs and that's on the right side. I was taken to the right side, whereas the windows for beatings are on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. On which floor was this office where you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably on that first floor. It was one flight up. The first floor compared to the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement and during the examination-in-chief, you said which persons were taken out and beaten. Did you see all these persons when they were taken out or did you hear about some of these persons being taken out from yet other persons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw all these persons being taken out and I mentioned them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also said that after some beatings and after some people were taken out, you heard gunshots as well. Where did these gunshots come from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, gunshots were heard every night within the compound of the KP Dom and around the KP Dom. People were shooting from various weapons. Why they were shooting, we don't know. However, the moment when the cries and screams stopped, at that point and in that area where they were beaten, gunshots were heard from there, individual gunshots. These were either pistols or rifles. It wasn't really bursts of gunfire. These were individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the statement that you made to the OTP you said that you heard shots that came from the direction of the bridge on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gunshots were heard from the bridge on the Drina as well. They were individual gunshots or bursts of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am reading this to you, and I am talking to you about the gunshots that you heard after the beatings stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There has been a very justifiable complaint made that you are going far, far too quickly, Mr. Bakrac. I know you want to get through this, but it doesn't get us anywhere. Now, we've lost the speed, I know. We certainly lost most of your question. So, please, would you repeat the question and do it more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you explained just now that you heard practically every night gunshots within the KP Dom and around the KP Dom. I'm talking specifically about the gunshots that you heard when the beatings stopped. So in relation to the incidents related to the beatings, you said that you heard individual gunshots. I'm asking you whether you agree that in your statement to the OTP you said that you heard these gunshots coming from the direction of the bridge on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. But gunshots were coming from the room where the beatings were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, what is correct now? Just now you said that you agreed that you heard gunshots coming from the bridge on the Drina River and then you added that you actually heard gunshots coming from the room for beatings.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are correct. Both are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement that you made to the OTP, you did not mention that you heard these gunshots coming from the room where the beatings were taking place.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I forgot. Perhaps I did not say this. But nobody interrogated me very precisely the way these interrogations in here are taking place, one detail after another. When I was giving my previous statements, these details were not is that precise, that exact when this statement was made. It's not like here, for instance, or before when I was interrogated that other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, we're not talking about precise or imprecise questions here. This is a specific fact that you are describing in different ways. So in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995, you said specifically that gunshots that are tied to the end of the beatings, in your opinion, came from the direction of the bridge on the Drina River. You did not mention that you heard these gunshots from the rooms for beatings.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I said that the gunshots came from the bridge on the Drina, that direction. Perhaps I did not mention this. Perhaps they did not write this down. But it is also correct that gunshots were heard from the room where the beatings took place. In addition to that, generally speaking, there were gunshots every evening within the compound, outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So these were gunshots that came from the rooms that you pointed to on the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you remembered that just now?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that then too. I never forgot that. I never forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you did not mention it earlier?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why did I not mention it? Perhaps I forgot. Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir, do you know Ismet Isakovic and Safet Avdic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ismet Isakovic, nicknamed Karson, born in Gorazde, was in my room. I know him. Safet Avdic, director, engineer, director of forestry from Maglic, he was also in my room. Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they in your room throughout your stay there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not there throughout my stay. They came from building 1. They came to my room. I don't know exactly. June, July. I don't know exactly. August. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In June, July, August, when they came to your room, until you were released were they in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but one group from my room was transferred and taken to the floor above. I don't know which room. And whether Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Karson and Safet Avdic were taken there too, I don't know, but I know about other people whom I can enumerate who were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, thank you. Please tell me: Do you know a guard by the name of Risto Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What kind of guard was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You spoke about the moment when you were taken for an exchange. You said, and I would like to repeat it for the benefit of the transcript -- did I understand you correctly as saying that a military truck came to pick you up, a military Deutz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that you were taken over by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you really say that these soldiers took away your watches, money, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This money and the watches, did you have them on you in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the KP Dom, I had no money, Rasim Kajgana gave me 5.000 dinars. He said, "You should have that." And as for the watch, I had it on my hand when I came to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You had a watch throughout the time you were in KP Dom and Rasim Kajgana gave you 5.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me turn your mind back to the interview you gave in Trnovo in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, would like to give the original, that's document ID 131 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you do not need to read this. I just would like to you have a look at it and identify your signature if you can.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Yes. This is exactly my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you look at this statement, it's three and a half pages, isn't it? If you look through it, just -- there are page numbers. Is it three and a half pages long?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You can put it aside, sir. I just -- do you remember how long this interview took? How long did it last.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That lasted for about a half a day. It took one afternoon, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you -- do you recall what you were focused on, what was the main subject of this questioning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well. The main subject they were interested in was how many detainees had remained in the camp. That was their main concern. They wanted me to enumerate the people by name and surname, and that was their main task, and they told me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also tell them in detail how you were arrested in Jelec and what beating and mistreatment you survived until you reached the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the details, but as far as I can remember, they did ask me that same thing. But they didn't ask about details. The interrogation went on very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also tell them about who was beaten in the KP Dom and who disappeared from the KP Dom and did you give a lot of names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. To the best of my recollection, I gave all those statements and they did inquire, but they said the main purpose of this questioning is to find out how many people remained there. And when I couldn't remember some people, they gave me time to think. That took up a lot of time. Sometimes I wouldn't be able to remember a first name or a last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you asked about the prison hierarchy at all on this occasion? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the main person was. I don't know exactly. They may have asked me, but I couldn't give you any details right now. They asked me about the warden. They may have and then maybe they didn't. I'm not sure about whether they asked me about the warden or the hierarchy. They didn't, in all probability.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, would the Defence agree that Krnojelac, Todovic or Rasevic, none of the prison hierarchy is mentioned in this statement at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is a saying in English, Mr. Bakrac, that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence agrees, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to the parties for following this procedure. It's one which I am very familiar with, and I think it is time it was introduced here in the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would the Defence also agree that the witness actually gave a lot of names of people who remained behind, and it's actually on page 4 of the English version, a chapter with great many names, and also on page 3 in the English version, a chapter with a lot of names of people who were beaten in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let's us now turn to the statement you gave to the OTP in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would also like to show this statement, the English version, and that is actually ID 130, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. I did sign this, but I had forgotten how these papers looked. I remembered only now. And my signature is really my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you look at the last page of the text, is it 14 pages?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I signed all of them. Those are my authentic signatures. All of this is correct. It's all right. Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember on what issues this interview was focused on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was giving this statement in 1995, what the focus was? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I start? They started from the beginning, how the war in Foca began, how things developed, where I moved about, how I was arrested, what the arrest looked like, how I was transferred to Foca. They asked me to tell things in their chronological order. In the process of questioning, they seemed to think that I was taking a long time and they asked me to be as brief as possible, to make it concise. So I shortened it and reached the point where I told them the story about my release and how I left Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would the Defence agree that the first nine pages of this statement, actually to the middle of the ninth page of the English version is dealing with the political background and what the witness had survived before his arrest in Jelec and after his arrest in Jelec until his arrival in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would the Defence agree that on page 12, the witness, about Mr. Krnojelac, said, "Mico Krnojelac was the head of the KP Dom Foca. His deputy was Gagovic," and so on, and does not mention Krnojelac at all any further except for on that same page in the last line and also in relation to Halim Konjo's death?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The Defence agrees with what the Prosecution is saying regarding references to Krnojelac, but the Prosecutor doesn't seem to have read that regarding the so-called administration of the KP Dom the witness also spoke about Mitar Rasevic, Todovic, investigators, et cetera. That is an entire paragraph relating to the structure of administration. I think the Prosecution will agree with this. So this has been read out only partially, but the entire paragraph relates to the structure of the administration, the persons employed there, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what it is that you're seeking to refer to there. Is there some other reference to your client, Mr. Krnojelac, by implication in that paragraph? As I understand it, the Prosecution is only seeking to demonstrate that the statement deals in a very minor way with your client. It doesn't go into anything about him very fully. Is what you are saying now that there is something in the statement beyond that to you which the Prosecution has referred concerning your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I agree that my client is mentioned, as the Prosecution says. He was the warden and his deputy was Gagovic. But the whole paragraph continues to deal with the administration and its structure. But we agree it is his statement and what the Prosecution has read out is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can read this paragraph it's actually just a ten-liner paragraph but I actually avoided to say it because it's so many names of guards in this paragraph and I'm not so good at pronouncing those names. Therefore, I actually did not read the whole entire paragraph. It's a paragraph dealing with all the people, the administration, of course, and the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your difficulty, which is very understandable, with the pronunciation of those names will therefore make you read it out more slowly so the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I can read this. The interpreters should have the statement as well and can look at it. "Mico Krnojelac was the head of KP Dom Foca. His deputy was Gagovic. The police commander at KP Dom was Mitar Rasevic (father's name Dorde). Todovic was the head of the workers in the KP Dom. The interrogators in the KP Dom were Zoran Paprica, Vojo Starevic, and Vladisic. The guards in KP Dom were Predrag Stefanovic 'Predo,' Cancar, Vladicic, Blagojevic, Zoran Matovic, Obren Obrenovic, Perisic, Elcic, Dobrilo Pljevaljcic, Roko, Micevic, Risto Ivanovic, Milivoje Milutinovic, Vukovic, Milic, Savic 'Kostolomac,' Miro Burilo, Prodanovic, Kunarac, Koroman, and Milic Mladenovic." Is that what you said? Is that okay? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And let me refer and ask Defence counsel in relation to page 10 in the English version, paragraph 2 -- or better I just read this. I think it's easier to read this. "The nights of 12/13 June and 22/23 June 1992 were the most" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you know where it is in the B/C/S version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's on page 9 and it's the seventh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "The nights of 12/13 June and 22/23 June 1992, were the most terrible. On 12 June at about 9/10 p.m., four prisoners were taken out. Their names are Halim Konjo, Nurko Nisic, Zulfo Veiz, and Munib Veiz. That day, Blagojevic, Elcic, and Vukovic were among the guards on duty and they were calling out and taking these prisoners to the administration building. On 18 June, I heard from [redacted] that the head of KP Dom, Krnojelac, told him that Halim Konjo had died in the solitary cell." I have mentioned the name. I'm sorry. I should have replaced it by his initials. "RJ was a former colleague teacher of Krnojelac and used to have coffee with him every ten days in KP Dom. I also heard later that the body of Munib Veiz was found at Gorazde in the Drina River." Do you agree that this is a reference to his conversation with RJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And there is yet another paragraph I would like to read out and have the Defence agree to, and that is actually the reference on page 9 to the interrogation of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version it's on page 9. It's the fourth paragraph in the B/C/S version. "Twenty to thirty days after I reached KP Dom, I was interrogated by Zoran Paprica and Vojo Starovic in the administration building. I was not beaten. I was never beaten in KP Dom." Would the Defence agree that this is the only reference in the statement related to the witness's interrogation and that it is followed by several pages of -- or pages of descriptions of beatings?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, The Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you came to The Hague to testify, was it actually the first time that you were asked in detail about where you saw Mr. Krnojelac, what you heard about him, and all the details you remembered related to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was summoned --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, I have an objection. When the Prosecution says details relating to him, I wish to say that earlier, Defence has already shown, through questions, that the witness had already spoken about facts which are now related to Milorad Krnojelac. If you put the question now this way, saying that the witness did not mention details related to Milorad Krnojelac, that sounds different. When he enumerated the members of the Crisis Staff, he didn't mention Krnojelac then. When he spoke about the visit of the journalists, he didn't mention Krnojelac then. He didn't mention the warden in his statements, but he did refer to Krnojelac in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think we've been over this ground many times. The way in which statements are taken by investigators, particularly in relation to the matters before this Tribunal, are they ask them everything they can about what happened. At that stage, there's no decision taken as to who is going to be charged. It's very different to what usually happens in domestic legal proceedings. After these statements have been compiled, then it is given to somebody who work out who is going to be charged. Now, the point you have made is a good one and one which will have to be considered, but the Prosecution are also entitled, you having raised that issue, to bring out in re-examination why it is that the witness is now giving us details not about what your client is now being asserted as having been involved in but his particular position in the KP Dom, and that is, as I understand it, what the question is directed to and that's another matter we're going to consider. But you can't criticise him for not giving these details before and then prevent the Prosecution from saying, "Well, this is the first time he's ever been asked about those sorts of details." That's all the Prosecution is doing, and fairness demands they should be entitled to do it. What weight we give to it is a different matter. Yes, you proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me repeat the question. Is it here in The Hague the first -- it is here for the first time that you are asked so specific questions about his -- your saying Krnojelac and his position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here before this Court specific questions. Not specific questions were asked about Krnojelac himself. I was asked to recount in chronological order what had happened and that's what I did, as far as I understood, to the best of my understanding. Questions were put to me like, "Was Krnojelac the warden of the KP Dom?" All of us who were in that camp, we know that he was the warden. That is indubitable. We knew that from the guards, from the inmates, and we all knew that Krnojelac was the warden of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, that was not my question. My question was: All these details that you were asked here in The Hague about when you saw him, what he was wearing, who he was with, is that the first time that you actually were asked all these details, here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you now. No, nobody had asked me questions like that before, questions like that in detail. They were not asked and I didn't answer them. They asked me in the sequence that I followed in my statements. They didn't ask me in such great detail as here. During earlier questionings, they didn't ask questions strictly about the warden. They asked me in general about my experience, what I had been, what it was like, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions that the Prosecution wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming here to give your evidence. Thank you for the evidence which you've given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Smith, is 122 the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. He's asked for no protective measures in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Amor Masovic. He's president of the State Commission for Tracing of Missing Persons in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, you should have received a folder this morning which is a revised version of a folder of documents that relate to this particular witness. Some documents have been removed from the original folder that was provided at the beginning of the case because they were deemed less relevant and a number of documents have been added which are quite relevant to his testimony. The folder -- the Defence has received a copy of the folder, and they've received the majority of the information a couple of weeks ago, and a document marked 240/5, which is a list of detainees at the KP Dom that are still recorded as missing with the commission, was provided to them last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We tried to get some agreement on the documents, Your Honour, but as a number of documents are summary documents, summaries of records held by the commission, because of the -- obviously the large amount of documentation that would be required to bring -- to substantiate each record, these summary documents have not at this stage been agreed to by the Defence. They want some more foundation as to their reliability before I think they will be in a position to either agree or not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that's the subject matter of the evidence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you keep talking to each other, counsel on each side, to see whether it is you can come to an agreement. It may be that Mr. Bakrac will want to cross-examine him before doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which is being handed to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I commence the questioning, the witness has a copy of the binder in front of him which are largely the documents or are the documents that have been produced by him and prepared by him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That should save a lot of time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, good morning. What is your full name and your professional occupation?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Amor Masovic is my name. I'm a lawyer by profession, and I hold the office of president of the State Commission for Searching for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm also chairman of the Federal Commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina for Searching for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you're also a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina parliament; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When was the State Commission for the Tracing of Missing Persons first established? What year?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It was established in the month of April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before April 1996, did the substance of that commission, the staff, did they operate under a different name?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Practically the entire staff of that commission operated under the name of The State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, Persons Deprived of Their Freedom, and also for keeping Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. records of missing and deceased persons on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the short title of that commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when was this State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, when was that first established?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992, the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the war, did the Serb authorities and the Croatian authorities also have similar commissions for the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did the -- when was the Serb commission established for the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Very soon, I think. I think in June or perhaps even the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when was the Croat commission established?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It was established even before that. It operated through the HVO, and I think it was established already before April because there had already been some clashes between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the HVO stands for the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In 1997, did the Croat commission and the Bosnian commission, did they join together under one political umbrella and become the Federal Commission for the Tracing of Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. In the month of July 1997, the federal commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established in which the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in practice, do the two commissions, the Croat commission and the Bosnian commission, do they operate relatively independently under this one umbrella?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: You can put it that way, that they operate independently, although they are formally the federal commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you first start work with the State Commission For the Exchange of Prisoners of War?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In August, in the second half of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what position did you have when you started?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: At first I was a member of that commission, then I was acting chairman, and finally until the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina ended I became president -- chairman of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in April 1996, were you appointed as president of the State Commission for the Tracing of Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The newly established commission for tracing missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the war, what was the main role and function of the State Commission for the Tracing of Prisoners of War? What was your main purpose?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, its main role is evident from its very name; that is to say, to trace persons who are in enemy prisons, and also persons who were deprived of their liberty during the conflict, also keeping records of the wounded and killed, as well as civilians and military persons who went missing during armed conflicts that occurred in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That is to say, in addition to keeping records, the task of the commission was to engage in negotiations with the enemy and to try to release from enemy prisons and camps the largest number of detained persons possible, especially civilians who had been taken prisoner or, rather, detain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the post-war period, say from 1996 onwards, did the nature of the commission's work change? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I did not get a translation. I only heard it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll just try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the post-war period, say from 1996 onwards, did the nature of the commission's work change compared to that of during the war?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way, yes. The State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War was primarily dealing with persons who were alive, persons who were taken prisoner; whereas this commission that deals with tracing missing persons unfortunately deals with persons who have probably died in the meantime. Most of these missing persons are basically dead now, so we are really looking for persons who lost their lives during the war because it's been such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And a large part of your work in the post-war period relates to conducting exhumations or coordinating exhumations in Bosnia to locate these missing people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you be more specific? What particular role does the commission play in the exhumation activity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The task of the commission is, on the basis of information that we compile from various sources, to locate individual and mass graves and then to give notification regarding these gravesites. That is to say, if we come to the conclusion that buried bodies are still within these graves, then we inform the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the state attorney, the courts, and persons from the state commission attend the exhumation itself. Sometimes we also attend the autopsies of the victims. Our task, finally, is to have contact with the families of the persons who are deceased when we assume that the victims we identified are the members of their families, and then we facilitate communication with these families and with the communities to which we assume the deceased persons belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what criteria does the commission use before it commences to activate an investigation into a possible exhumation site in terms of whether there was evidence of a war crime or a person dying of natural or unnatural causes?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I said that we use all possible sources that can lead us to a locality where a certain number of persons was buried, one or more persons. When speaking of these sources, we primarily establish contact with family members of missing persons, then also with possible witnesses, regardless of whether these are direct witnesses, immediate witnesses who were present during the liquidation and who managed to survive, or indirect witnesses, persons who found out indirectly that there are individual or mass graves. Also, we rely on other sources apart from family members, that is to say, police reports, court reports, information provided by the International Red Cross, information provided by local Red Cross organisations, and also data that we receive from local commissions or, rather, local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your authority to instigate investigations into possible exhumation sites, I assume that only relates to deaths that are suspected of being of unnatural causes rather than natural causes?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. We are duty-bound, along the lines of the decision that was passed by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to establish this commission, to investigate these cases; that is to say, cases related to persons who went missing during the conflict and when we are talking about persons who were killed during the war. We do not deal with persons who possibly died during the course of 1992 or 1993 due to natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the post-war period, from 1996 onwards, what relationship does your commission have with the Croat part of the federal commission and the Serb commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from 1996 onwards, formally, legally speaking, there are still two commissions, the state commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the commission on the exchange of prisoners of war that is still attached to the Croatian army known as the HVO. In 1997 a separate commission, a separate entity commission was established which is called the Federal Commission For Missing Persons. That happened in 1997. And I already said formally, legally, there has been one commission since then, and this part does function rather autonomously, this part which represents the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In 1996, there was an agreement made between the Croat commission- this is before it became the federal commission - and the Bosnian Serb -- the Republika Srpska commission in relation to exhumations. And what was the basis of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That agreement is known as the Banja Luka agreement. It was concluded in Banja Luka in Republika Srpska in June 1996. It was initiated by the representatives of the office of the high representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it involved all three former warring parties, that is to say, the state commission, the commission of the Croat Defence Council, and the commission of Republika Srpska. The essence of this agreement has to deal with exhumations. It makes it possible for the authorities of one entity to cross the administrative border into the other entity and to engage in exhumation on the territory of the other entity. That is the essence of this agreement. So, for example, the Serb commission can come to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the territory of Republika Srpska, that is to say, to the territory of the Bosnian-Croat Federation, and that on that territory they can carry out all necessary actions related to exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in practice, does the Republika Srpska commission and the Bosniak part of the federal commission and the Croat part of the federal commission, do they largely deal with the exhumations of people of the same ethnicity as the commission entity?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb commission only deals with Serb victims, that is to say, where the victims were Bosnian Serbs. The state commission or, rather, the Federal Commission for Tracing Missing Persons deals with all victims but predominantly, predominantly those victims that belong to the ethnic groups that this federation relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Since the war, how many Bosnian Muslims have been exhumed in Bosnia? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We can say that this number is about 10.500. I think that 6.500 were exhumed by the State Commission For Tracing Missing Persons and about 4.000 were exhumed by representatives of the Tribunal. I'm referring to the Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know how many Bosnian Serb victims have been exhumed? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have the relevant information, but according to some information that I do have, this number ranges between 1.200 and 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: About 500. A bit less than 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During the war, what was the relationship between the three commissions in terms of the exchange of prisoners? Did you have much contact?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Very frequent contact. Sometimes this was once a week, on neutral territory, that is to say, territory that was under the control of UN forces known as UNPROFOR or perhaps at the lines of conflict or, rather, the separation lines between the military forces. That is where these contacts took place, and they were very frequent, as I said, or at any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rate, far more frequent than any other contacts that took place between the then warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the war, did you represent the Bosnian state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was its vice-chairman. But in fact, I was the person who was engaged in fieldwork the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when prisoners exchanges were organised, who would you deal with from the Serb commission or the Croat commission in terms of the hierarchy? Would you deal with the head of those commissions or would you deal with the people with the custody of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively with persons who were authorised by the other side to act on behalf of their commissions that had different names. The Serb commission was called the Central Commission and the Croat commission was called the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, only their commissions, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you didn't deal with the people that physically captured the detainees in a direct sense?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. We did not have access at all to detention facilities, that is to say, to camps or prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the war, was there a headquarters for the state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, the headquarters of the state commission was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there any local or regional offices that formed part of that state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, during the second half of the war, that is to say, from 1993 all the way until the end of the war, there were separate departments of the state commission that were established in various towns that were under government forces control. Gorazde, Tuzla, Bihac, Mostar, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the staff size of the state commission, say, in 1992 when you started in August? How many staff were there?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think in that period, between 12 and 15 people were employed in the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1992, when you started, were they based in the Sarajevo office or were some of them based somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, at the headquarters of the commission in Sarajevo, there were about seven persons employed, I think, and some were in the field, that is to say, in the towns that I mentioned and also Trnovo, for instance, then also Ilidza, Hadzici, Konjic, and I think a few other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is the staff size of the state commission or the Bosniak part of the federal commission for the tracing of missing persons basically the same as when it started now as when it started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Nowadays, we have 15 employees, persons who are full-time employees there, and we have volunteer, that is to say, a person who cooperates with the commission but that is not formally employed as a full-time employee of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And currently of the 15 employees, about how many are based in the Sarajevo office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Seven, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And have you always been based at the headquarters office in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: From August 1992 until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And does the office keep records of people exhumed and people that are missing, recorded as missing?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During the war, what type of records were kept, just generally, in relation to prisoners of war, missing people?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Practically our first sources or, rather, if we're talking about records, I already said during my introductory remarks that we have recorded prisoners of war, persons who were deprived of their liberty in relation to the armed conflict and also persons who were wounded or killed during a certain period of time and, finally, persons who went missing. During the war, records related to the killed and wounded were taken over by other authorities such as the Ministry of Health, whereas we continued to record prisoners of war, persons deprived of their liberty and also persons who went missing during the war conflict. And finally, in the period after the general peace agreement was signed in Dayton, we have been keeping records related to exhumed persons since exhumations were made possible, conditionally speaking, on enemy territory only after the Dayton Accords were signed. During the war, we did not have access to localities where civilians or soldiers were killed within the territory that was under enemy control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in this post-war period, you still keep records of missing people?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are these records centralised in the headquarters office or had they spread throughout the regional offices as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Records were centralised; that is to say, all information comes to our headquarters in Sarajevo. And records are also kept on missing persons in certain regions but persons who gravitate towards that particular region. For example, our office in Tuzla, to the north of Sarajevo, keeps records of persons who went missing on the territory of Republika Srpska, which does gravitate towards Tuzla. For example, Srebrenica, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Bijeljina, and some other towns also. In some of our other offices, records are kept that are of a local nature. However, all information, all data do ultimately reach the headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we go though, I don't know whether we are required to read all of these Sarajevo court files, et cetera, but they are all in B/C/S and there is no, except in relation to documents 8 and 9, there are no translations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage we don't propose to tender these records. They may become relevant subject to opposing counsel's view of the records, and there is summary translations, but think stage we propose not to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as you realise that we haven't been given the wrong file. It has happened. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, before the break you talked about how records in relation to prisoners of war and missing persons were centralised into the headquarters office in Sarajevo during the war. You also said that regional offices were set up on a permanent basis in 1993 and that in 1992, you believe that some of the staff from the state commission were actually working in the field in some places such as Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During that 1992 period, from when the war broke out in Bosnia, say, from April 1992, to the end, were you receiving information from these staff members in the field in relation to prisoners of war and missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a continuous flow of such data practically from the beginning of the war, from April 1992, from the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, including that department, the regional, the Municipal Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were these regional commissions, were they obliged to provide the information to the Sarajevo office as a matter of course, as a matter of duty?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. They were duty-bound not only to keep their own records but also to forward to the central headquarters in Sarajevo all data related to the exchange of prisoners of war and any bodies revealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the records kept regarding exhumations and missing persons, have you recently been asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to summarise those records from the source material that you have at your office in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have those summarised documents with you today?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to exhumations, can you tell the Court what type of records you kept?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I should mention that exhumations are primarily related to the status of missing persons. In my introductory remarks, I said that regrettably today, eight years after the beginning of the war, almost all missing persons or even all missing persons are actually dead. They were killed during the war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and further afield, in the territory of Yugoslavia, so that actually, data related to exhumations has been collected since 1992. Already since 1992 we recorded the first missing persons, the first murders of civilians and soldiers, and in the post-war period, after the Banja Luka agreement of 1996 on interentity exhumations, we started exhumations in the territories held during the war by Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Croats, and we commenced with exhumations of individual and mass graves in which we are beginning to uncover the bodies of persons which are registered as missing in our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in relation to your records, what type of records do you keep? For example, do you keep court files or police files or any other type of record of exhumations? What range of records do you keep? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have a computer database which contains some basic details of a missing person or if the person's body is exhumated, data about the exhumation, and that means their name and surname of the missing or exhumed person, the father's name, year of birth, place of birth, place of residence, the date and place where the person was last seen, and if the person has been registered by the ICRC, then you would also find in our database the so-called BAS number, the code name under which that person is registered in the records of the ICRC and some additional remark related to events subsequent to the report when the person was reported as missing, and if the body was exhumed, then we also have information on the exhumations. In addition to this data, our database also contains written reports we received during the war and after the war from our commissions or commission departments but also from other authorities, local authorities, the police, intelligence, agencies, War Presidencies, municipalities, the International Red Cross, and some other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you also keep some of the court files in relation to exhumations conducted?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Once a year, after the exhumations for that year are finalised, the so-called annual report is made available to the commission, the annual report on exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When Bosnian Muslim civilians are exhumed, does someone from the commission attend at the exhumation site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Always, without exception. Members of the state commission always attend exhumations, either from the central commission in Sarajevo or from a department in Gorazde, Tuzla, Zenica, Travnik, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is there any requirement for the staff member that attends the exhumation site to make some interim in-house report as to what happened and the results of the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that report, the staff member would typically indicate the name of the locality where the exhumation was conducted, including the microlocation, the coordinates of that locality, the type of grave such as an individual grave or a grave containing five bodies or a mass grave, which means five or more corpses, and if identification has been made, the report also indicates the presumed identity. Identification is finalised by the cantonal court, but we always indicate the presumed identity, to be confirmed by subsequent procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does the Bosnian government expect you to keep records of the work that you do in relation to missing persons and exhumations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is our obligation to keep those records and to report to the government once a year on the results of the exhumations and our search for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the exhumations that have been conducted in the Foca municipality, I would like to show you a document. It's a map. It's numbered 240/1, Prosecution identification number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whilst that is being done, Mr. Smith, are we going to hear anything about the subsequent procedures to confirm the presumed identity?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, if you look at that document marked 240/1, which is placed next to you on the overhead projector, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map of prewar borders of the Foca municipality, indicating localities where exhumations have been conducted. They are grouped in about ten different localities which are actually local communes. Sometimes it's one local commune, sometimes more than one. We see here indicated the number of localities and the number of victims exhumed in these localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was this map prepared by the staff in your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was prepared by the staff of the state commission, headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if the map can be left on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now I'd ask you to look at the next document, a document also marked 240/1, which is an index which relates to the map. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you just briefly explain how the document relates to the map?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This document indicates ten different groups of sites where exhumations of victims from the municipality of Foca were conducted from 1996 to the year 2000. I have already said that it contains the ordinal number of the locality, then the name of the village or town where exhumation was conducted, microlocation, if any, the number of bodies uncovered, and the number of identified and unidentified bodies. This division is based according to the local communes to which the victims belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have this index prepared under your direction?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We compiled this index in the form in which you see it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be harping on this, Mr. Smith, but does the word "identified" there mean finally or provisionally or presumably?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Finally identified, Your Honour. There's another list, which is 240/3, which relates to the identifications of 375 of the 430 bodies. I think he will explain about how those people were identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I only wanted to know whether it was the provisional identification or, I'm sorry, the presumed identity, a phrase which worried me a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll clarify with the witness, but it's final identity, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, if you now look at document marked 240/3, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What does that document show?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list of victims identified in the territory of the Foca municipality, victims exhumed and identified. This list contains the names of 375 identified victims which were exhumed between 1996 and 2000 in the territory of the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can briefly ask you, how were those people identified, those 375? What process was undertaken to identify these people?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The victims were identified -- are identified by a special commission headed by a judge of the cantonal court and which includes the prosecutor and forensics of the police and also a forensic medical expert and his assistant. In this case, identification was done based on recognition by family members who came to the morgue or the prosecutor's office; and there, based on personal items found on the body, clothing, footwear, or certain characteristics such as fractures sustained before the conflict, identification was made on that basis. What we have here in this document is a relatively high percentage of identification of female persons. On the average, there are 12 per cent of women among the identified victims. Here this percentage is higher. It's 40 per cent, which means 145 victims of female sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So the identifications made in relation to these 375 are confirmed identifications, not presumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This, what we have here is a definitively -- is definitive identification, certified by an authorised forensic medical expert or coroner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We've finished with the documents for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the types of source material that were used to compile these documents, are they the same materials that you referred to earlier, such as --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who provided the source material for these documents, for these summary documents?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The background material originates from the state commission, and our sources are court reports, police reports that we receive, and also reports by forensic medical experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And reports from your staff who have attended at these exhumations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Those are our in-house reports compiled by staff members of the state commission who attend exhumations, autopsies, and identifications of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long after an exhumation is conducted would you start to receive the material which is the source for these documents?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That depends primarily on the number of victims exhumed from a particular grave. If it's a mass grave, as was the case with some graves where we found more than a hundred victims, then the time lapse is a bit longer. It could be up to 30 days. In other cases, when the number of bodies is smaller, then our in-house reports arrive on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the Foca municipality, how many -- other than documents that you receive at your office, have you been personally involved in some of the exhumations in the Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally attended, as leader of the team of the state commission, a number of exhumations conducted on the territory of the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to documents regarding exhumations received at your office, do you view those documents as they come into your office or do they go into a file and do you not see them?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All reports on completed exhumations pass through my hands, so to speak, and only after I verify them are the basic elements of these reports entered into our computer database.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in preparation for your testimony today, have you familiarised yourself with the source material used in these summary documents?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We used written material that we had available, court reports, witness statements when they were available, exhumation reports and reports made by War Presidencies and local commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just ask you a few questions now about the results of the exhumations in the Foca municipality. How many bodies have been exhumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In 156 different localities, which are grouped in ten groups of localities, the total of victims exhumed amounts to 436 for the period between 1996 and the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that 375 of those bodies have been identified, which means that 55 are still unidentified.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, 55 victims have not yet been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 375 that have been identified, has anyone been identified as a former detainee of the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In two cases, we found that the victim had last been seen in the correctional detention centre in Foca, in the KP Dom, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the names of those two individuals?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Those are Murat Crneta and Halid Konjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, these two individuals are referred to in Prosecution Exhibit P55/2, and at tab 13 in the folder there are excerpts from the Gorazde court in relation to this exhumation. Those excerpts, in fact, come from the exhibit 55/2, except the fuller translation has now Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you present at this exhumation site of the former detainees, Murat Crneta and Halid Konjo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Smith, to interrupt, but where is tab 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In part B of the folder, Your Honour. It's the last tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not fortunate enough to have numbers, but it's 55/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: /2, but it has been copied, recopied, and placed in the folder before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map in front of you the location to where these bodies where exhumed, Halid Konjo's and Murat Crneta's, with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can show the exact locality where we exhumed these two former detainees of the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you're pointing at the village of Previla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Previla, north of Foca town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's in group 2 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were these two men located with any other bodies?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, this was a mass grave where seven victims were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when were they exhumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think this was the month of November 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what information did you and the authorities have to lead you to this site to discover these bodies?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: One of the local Bosnian Serbs was in contact with the Gorazde police, and he discovered a group of 12 detainees moving in the vicinity of his house. They had been escorted. Immediately after that, he heard some shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did this person say when, when this occurred, what year or what date?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly the police in Gorazde was told about this, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the exhumation site when you arrived there and the state of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A forest path moves -- goes to Previla, and about 50 metres off that path there is a brook which dries up very often, and only in the spring and in the late autumn is there water in this brook. So in that area that is roughly three metres wide and ten metres long, so this is about 30 square metres altogether, that is where we located the incomplete remains of the skeletons of a total of seven victims. It was the court from Gorazde that was involved, with the assistance of forensic experts from Foca and with the assistance of Mrs. Simmons, a forensics expert from the United States. The skeletons were not complete because the water had washed away some of the smaller bones belonging to these skeletons. Some of the bones had been scattered about. It's probably animals that took them away, because five years had elapsed since the liquidation of these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you conclude from the scene how they died?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think, in view of the statement made by this witness and in view of the forensic expertise, forensic expertise established that they were executed by a firing squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were bullets found at the scene?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall right now whether there were any bullets at this locality. I think that this exists in the police report that was drafted by the Gorazde police, since it is policemen who take care of that part of such exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were these bodies buried or found on the surface?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It was obvious there on the spot that these bodies had not been buried, that the liquidation had occurred at the same spot, that is to say, in the bed of that brook, and that the bodies remained in the bed of that brook that had dried up. I come to this conclusion because parts of the skeletons were found in the sand and mud. Also, there were pebbles that covered parts of the skeletons, and it is probably towards the water that came subsequently that brought all these pebbles over the course of these five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who identified Murat Crneta and Halid Konjo?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Halid Konjo was identified by his wife. Murat Crneta was identified by his father-in-law, that is to say, his wife's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And both of those men were Bosnian Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from the Gorazde cantonal court report, the exhumation report, can it be seen that an identification card from a Sulejman Celik was found at the exhumation site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Celik, his identification card was found deep down in the mud, as far as I can recall, at a depth at 20 or 30 centimetres in the mud. As we were searching the mud, we found some smaller bones, like finger bones and toe bones. That's when we found this card. I remember the card very well. It was a membership card of the trade unions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the name on the card was Sulejman Celik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is he recorded as missing, with your state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is recorded with the state commission as one of the persons who are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, these three individuals who have been identified, at least the card of one of them, and the other two, evidence has been presented in this case that they were all taken out for this plum-picking incident in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did they need their trade union card for that job? Is seems a strange thing for them to have kept while they were in custody, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 375 identified bodies, you mentioned that there was a high number of females. About how many of them were females? What was the number?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thirty-nine per cent. I said a few minutes ago that this is indeed a high percentage as compared to the average percentage of women that we have exhumed so far, and we have exhumed over 6.500 victims. The average percentage of women exhumed was 12 per cent. However, in the territory of the municipality of Foca, we managed to exhume 39 per cent, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the 375 that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 375 victims, 374 are Bosnian Muslims and one woman is Montenegrin by origin, and she was married to a Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What is her name?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Srnja, nee Micunovic, Jelena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: She appears, Your Honour, at 309 on document 240/3

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 55 unidentified bodies, do the circumstances indicate what ethnicity those people were?
