utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be assumed beyond any reasonable doubt that these are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how can you assume that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The victims were located and exhumed in the villages where Bosnian Muslims lived in the territory of the municipality of Foca. Judging by their clothes, especially women's clothes, it is obvious that this was the Bosnian Muslim national costume, and also witnesses who survived these executions lead to the conclusion that these are Bosniaks or, rather, Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You have recorded in your document that 24 bodies were exhumed from a location in Ratine. This is on page 3, line 9, and it's exhumation site 107. It's on 340/1. It's page 3 of your index.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Line 9, and the site is 107.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the locality of Ratine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's recorded there that 24 people were exhumed or bodies were exhumed, but no one was identified. Did you attend that exhumation site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you point out the site on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The witness indicates Ratine in group 6 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What information did you have or the authorities have to lead you to this location at Ratine where the 24 bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, it was a mass execution that was survived by one of those persons who were shot at by automatic weapons. After the war, he took one of my officials from the state commission to that particular site and told him about that site where the execution took place. It was detainees who were in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These detainees, where were they from? Where did he say they were from?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I can be very precise, but I think these were detainees from Kalinovik. They were driven to this locality on two buses or two trucks, and then one of these trucks or buses was stopped. Twenty-five detainees were taken out, including the witness, and that's where the witness saw the execution of these detainees. The other truck continued its journey, and we haven't been able to locate those victims yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he say whether the victims were Serb or Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The witness is exactly aware of the identity of all 24 victims, and he dictated this list of victims containing their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All were Bosnian Muslims, and the witness had known them from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did he say that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but my official who was on the ground may know of that particular detail too. I can only say that the year was 1992, but I do not know a more specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly, can you say what you saw when you arrived at the site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Fifty or 60 metres below the road where we parked our vehicles, we came across the remains of a barn. Actually, these were only the foundations of a barn. The foundations were made of stone, natural stone. Within that barn there were about 20 or 30 metal sheets that were made of barrels. These sheets are made when a barrel is cut up and flattened. That's what the barn had been made of, apparently. When we came, we saw that there was grass and bushes growing all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 430 bodies that were exhumed in the Foca municipality, can you say, from your records, where their former residences were? Did they live in Foca or did they live somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All of them or almost all of them lived in the territory of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipality of Foca in 1991. We checked this against the census that was carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991. Also on the basis of the family members who identified them told us and on the basis of the census, I can say that all of them or a vast majority of them were inhabitants of Foca in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the basis of the exhumation records, are you able to say where -- are there any conclusions that you can draw in relation to where the bodies were exhumed with regards to their homes, their residences?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to conclude, from the information that you've got, how far away the residences were of the bodies that were exhumed? How far away were their homes?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: There is no one there. This is a forest path where wood is taken out of the forest, and I'm sure that these persons were obviously far away from their homes, although they are from the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now talking about the vast majority of the people that were exhumed in Foca. Can you draw any conclusions as to whether they were exhumed near their homes or far away from them?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All the exhumed were in the municipality of Foca, and most of them were exhumed where they had lived, some of them even in their homes or in front of their homes, within their own land. We inferred that these persons had actually stayed at home on their land, not fearing that they would be killed. However, nowadays we can regrettably say they made a mistake. So most of them were found in villages, hamlets, at their homes, in front of their homes, in their barns, and on their own land, primarily in those parts of the municipalities of Foca where the population is predominantly Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From the information you have from your records, is there a common time when these people were in fact killed or died?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be stated with certainty that most of them were killed in the period between April and the end of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was the most common cause of death?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The most common cause of death are multiple gunshot exit/entry wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From your knowledge of the records, about what percentage of the people were executed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It is hard to give precise information. However, speaking in terms of percentage, I think that over 90 per cent of the victims involved were executed in mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Approximately how did the other 10 per cent die, from the records?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can give you precise figures about the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not Foca only. There were different forms of liquidation that were established by forensics experts. Automatic weapons, executions by automatic weapons, and then also shooting people into their head directly or neck. We also found cases where persons' throats were slit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Masovic. If you can confine your answer to the Foca municipality and the other 10 per cent that you say, from the records weren't executed, do you know the cause of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In all cases, practically all cases, with the exception of a very few where we established natural causes of death, where forensics experts established natural causes of death, death was -- so in all cases, death was a result of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've also recorded in your index at 240/1 that nine people were exhumed from a site called Mazoce. This is on page 5, line 10. Also, at line 11, another two people were killed at the village of Mazoce. Did you attend this execution site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the locality of Ratine, number 121, where nine victims were exhumed, I was present there; and I was also present at yet another location where two victims were exhumed. This is also the area of Mazoce. I'm sorry, locations 91 and 92, those are the numbers that we gave in the state commission. Mazoce 1, nine victims; Mazoce 2, two victims; and I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you see at this particular site where the nine victims were found? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The locality Mazoce 1, nine victims buried in a mass grave in an orchard. After the autopsy, it was determined that all of them were executed by gunfire, and after identification, it was established that these were the members of a family whose last name was Rikalo at the location of Mazoce, the first one, Mazoce 1. As far as I can remember, two of the victims were women at the location of Mazoce 2. They were exhumed underneath a tree. I think it was a plum tree. These were two men [as interpreted] who had been buried together and covered with a metal sheet, or, rather, the remains of an automobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of these people who were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All were identified and all are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did they come from that village of Mazoce?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, prewar inhabitants of the village of Mazoce who had stayed at their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you indicate the village of Mazoce on the map?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The witness indicates Mazoce in group 10 on 240/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many houses were in the village of Mazoce?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It is hard to say. We found houses that were partly burned, partly torched; some were intact. But I would not say that there were over 25 or 30 houses at the location where we were, that is to say, near that orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Mazoce, did you meet a resident from there, from that village?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We were actually accompanied by the family members of these persons who we were looking for, who we managed to exhume and identify. Nowadays they do not live in Mazoce, but they live in other places of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, they accompanied us on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did they draw any conclusion as to houses that -- the reason why certain houses were torched or burnt, partly torched or burnt, and why others were left untouched?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The daughter of one of the victims drew my attention to the fact that the houses of all of those or most of those persons who were killed and who we exhumed on that occasion were intact, that their houses were not burned, that they were actually intact; whereas the houses of all of those who in 1992, under assaults of the Serb army, managed to flee to free territory or to Montenegro, that their houses were razed to the ground, that their houses had actually been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, apart from the woman that was exhumed, the Serb woman that was the wife to a Muslim male, apart from her being exhumed in this 375, you said that the rest that were exhumed were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There was no translation there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. There was something wrong with my microphone. Apparently it wasn't on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you recall, or would you like to have the answer again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, I would like to have the answer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you to start again, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, apart from the woman of Serb ethnicity in the 375 identified people exhumed from Foca, the rest that were exhumed were of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three hundred seventy-four were Bosnian Muslims, and it is beyond any reasonable doubt that I can confirm that the remaining 55 belonged to the Bosnian Muslim population, those who have not been identified until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Other than this woman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know that the witness says beyond reasonable doubt, but should we know the basis upon which he comes to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He is a lawyer by trade, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that, and he would understand what the word means, but we have to make up our own minds. I don't want him to go into a great deal of detail, but there must be some explanation he can give us shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He has given an explanation previously, but if I can just get him to summarise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The last time it was the clothing that they wore in the villages in which they had resided and that sort of thing; and if it's the same, he can say it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why can you say in your mind beyond a reasonable doubt that these 55 are of Muslim ethnicity, these other 55 bodies? What's your basis for that? If it's nothing more than what you said before, then just say that.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I said earlier, and I can confirm it again, the witnesses who brought us to the site of liquidation, the place where we find those identified bodies, claimed that the victims were Bosnian Muslims. The same can be concluded based on their clothing and on the basis of the fact that they originate from villages populated by Bosnian Muslims. That is my conclusion, and in my mind, it is beyond any reasonable doubt that they are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't mean to challenge that, sir, but you can be, I think, of a little bit more assistance to us. Did the persons who identified them as Bosnian Muslims claim to be able to identify them as people they had known?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In certain cases, yes. But in the process of identification, family members who attended the identification were not able to confirm with certainty that those were actually their family members, because part of the corpses were incinerated, other parts had no characteristic features to enable identification. So in certain cases, such as the case of the barn in Ratine containing 24 corpses, we know precisely and for sure who the persons were. But since the bodies were incinerated after executions, all we have are the remains of their skeletons. Now, forensics were not able to state with certainty which part of which skeleton belongs to which victim. So these 24 victims remain recorded as unidentified, but we know for a fact that they were Bosnian Muslims because one person who is a survivor of the same incident confirms it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, you did tell us that before. And to some extent, I suppose, you have had to rely upon the fact that if there were a large number of persons identified in this way as being Bosnian Muslims, the fact that the others were with them, you have assumed that they were also Bosnian Muslims; is that so?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I would say it's more than an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What would you say it was, then?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We can assume, based on all the relevant data at our disposal, that these are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Smith, I'll leave it to you. That's still Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an assumption, to my mind, and I think the witness used the word. I'm thinking of evidence I've heard in other cases, that's all, and the way in which it's been proven, and that was one of the issues that was taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think he's probably said as much as he can on the topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Other than the woman of Serb ethnicity, are you aware of any non-Muslims being exhumed in the Foca municipality; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to talk about the records that you keep in relation to missing persons. What type of records do you keep to record that someone is missing, with your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: There is a computer database, first of all, compiled based on elements derived from oral reports or from reports made by family members or from other sources such as records made by the ICRC or lists which we received throughout the war and after the war from local authorities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have records from the police or military in relation to missing persons as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In one part of written material, which means court, police, and other reports available to the prosecutor's office, are intelligence and military reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you have witness statements as well as part of your record in relation to missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, witness statements or statements by family members who in certain cases happen also to be witnesses of incidents in which a person went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said earlier that your organisation has a duty to keep records in relation to exhumations. Do you also have a similar duty to keep full records in relation to missing persons reported?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what use is made -- is there any use made of the records that you keep at your office for anything other than court purposes? Does the government use your records for any particular reason? Do they rely on your records, or do any other organisations rely on your records in relation to missing persons, for their own use?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, these records are of service to the families of the missing persons, because after a filing a report that a person is missing, they receive from us a certificate to the effect that a member of their family went missing. And based on that certificate, local authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina grant them certain benefits for surviving family members. And based on the same records, certain international organisations which deal in migration or immigration into western countries grant preferential treatment to certain categories of the Bosnian population, and I mean primarily surviving family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do any other organisations use your records for any other purposes, or any purposes, like Red Cross, for example, or ...

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: At the request of local cantonal courts and prosecutors' offices, we make available our own data on missing persons to be used in trials on war crimes before international courts and Tribunals, and we also reply to requests filed by individual families through the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at document number 240/4. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what does the document show?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a list of currently recorded missing persons, that is, missing persons currently on record from the Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was this list prepared under your instruction at the state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on my instructions and based on our records and data on such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can look at a document marked 240/5. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My office drafted this document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what does that document show?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This is one part of persons recorded as missing in Foca municipality, persons last seen in the KP Dom of Foca. Their number is 265.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you look at the last page of the document, the number appears to be 266.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said in your previous answer that the number is 265. Is that correct or is it 266?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said 266. It may be the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's clear now. Thank you. In order to produce this document, how many sources were used for each individual person to come at this conclusion that they were at KP Dom and they are recorded as still missing? How many sources did you use to support each entry in this document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We used at least two sources, and in certain cases we used as many as four independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there any people from your records that are not included in this document that you have recorded as missing from KP Dom -- sorry, you have recorded as being at KP Dom and still missing in addition to these 266?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On our records, I believe there are at least 35 persons recorded as last seen in the KP Dom in Foca. However, from two -- at least two independent sources, we could confirm that they went missing in the KP Dom of Foca. So this list of 266 names do not include these 35 persons, although they were last seen in the Foca KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the 730 from the Foca municipality in total that you have recorded as missing, when did the majority of these people go missing or were reported to you as having gone missing? From what year?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Reports have been filed continuously from the outbreak of the conflict, and beginning with 1993, we have complete records of persons who went missing on the territory of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is there a common time period where the majority of these people have gone missing?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: From the first half of April until end September 1992, a small number of them, I think less than 20, went missing in the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long in relation to the 730 people who are missing, how long after they have gone? How long after you have known that they went missing would the report have been made?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation varies. Sometimes on the same day, when a person was taken away, he is recorded as missing as of the day he was taken away from his home, and on average, I believe the time period is 15 or 30 days between the time when the person went missing and the time of filing of the reports and entry into our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved personally in receiving these reports as to missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All reports go through my hands before the basic elements of the reports are entered into our computer database. But in some cases where witnesses appeared who could testify on a larger number of missing persons who went missing in one and the same day, I questioned those witnesses. In other cases where less complicated testimonies were involved, my assistants handled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Say in the 1992 period, throughout the war, how many staff members did you have receiving reports of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Six members in the central commission in Sarajevo, and I believe between eight and ten staff members who were on missions at various localities controlled by various forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that reports were made orally and in writing. Who would generally make the oral reports as to a missing person?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We can call this a report, but oral reports of disappearance were usually made by family members or witnesses of incidents that preceded the disappearance of the person, whereas written reports were made by prosecution authorities, military police authorities, various commissions for exchanges of prisoners of war, War Presidencies, municipalities in wartime and perhaps some other state authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The family members that made reports of missing persons, did they come to your office in person or was it made over the phone? Was there a predominance of what one type of reporting or another?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That depended on where the disappearance occurred. If a person went missing on the territory where family members or witnesses had access to our headquarters in Sarajevo, then that would occur in our headquarters in Sarajevo. But if a person went missing elsewhere, in different territories, then oral reports would be forwarded to our regional departments in towns which I enumerated before, Mostar, Tuzla, Travnik, Zenica, Hadzici, Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you get the heart of the answer? Yes. Sir, the interpreters have complained that you are speaking a little quickly. Could you slow down when you're giving your answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about 45 minutes left of his testimony, but my colleague has a couple of applications to make in relation to witnesses following, so I wonder whether or not we could make those applications now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly. Well, Mr. Masovic, we'll let you go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Hunt, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, we'll let you go now. They want to raise a few matters before we adjourn. We resume at 9.30 in the morning. We'll see you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are these your applications, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. One of the matters can be discussed in open session, but the other I would request a private session. The first matter relates to the witness 137, who is scheduled for next week videolink, and the Office of the Prosecutor has contacted this witness today and the witness has consulted a doctor, and he is now able to travel. He receives other medications, and because of the change of the weather and because of his present condition, he's able to travel now, and he is available to testify here in The Hague. I think it's more preferable to have him here if he can travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you holding out that the weather here in The Hague will be as good next week as it is this week?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The problem is the witness suffers from rheumatism, and except for the fact that he gets now medication, different medication, the weather in the area where he lives now has now turned to spring and it is warmer, and, therefore, he has recovered. His physical condition is much better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if he can come, it's obviously better that he does come, that's for sure. I'm sure Mr. Bakrac would not dispute that. Very well. Then what do you want us to do, cancel an order for the videolink?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this witness but not in relation to the other because we have two witnesses in Sarajevo and the other one cannot travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When do you anticipate bringing 137 along?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Next week. He will testify in person next week on the same day, actually, as he was schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the trip for our Court Deputy will not be lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then. Well, do we need to actually make a fresh order or just we can make an order now deleting the reference to witness 137 for the -- from the order for a videolink next week. Thank you. Now, the other matter you want private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. For the other matter I would like to have private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of March, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
